This series of policy changes cast Ontario into a position where it either had to attempt to recoup the damage done through uploading responsibilities back to the province, provide additional revenue streams for municipalities, or tacitly stealth downloads through a variety of means including incrementalism. After Dalton McGuinty's Liberals took power in late 2003, several policies impacting local government were introduced. First, the Province set out a plan to invest more than 680 million sourced from its gas tax into 78 different transit systems across 105 of Ontario's municipalities by the end of 2006. Municipalities would begin receiving 1 per litre of this gas tax, which would increase up to 2 (Office of the Premier, 2004). Next, the creation of the Ontario Municipal Partnership Fund, featuring an unconditional equalization program, catered to Third, the McGuinty government explicitly addressed the mistake of downloading caused by Harris era policies and promised to absorb nearly 935 million in social services costs that were previously the responsibility of local governments (CBC News, 2007). Last, the Provincial Municipal Fiscal and Service Delivery Review recommended the expenses for social assistance (Ontario Works), the Ontario Disability Support Program, seniors' prescriptions, and court security costs be uploaded from local Although some programs were uploaded to the provincial government, other initiatives under the McGuinty government were either downloaded to local governments or the authority of local governments was suspended. The McGuinty government removed the capacity for local governments to control wind farm development projects as part of the province's Green Energy Act. In an attempt to create efficient approval processes for renewable energy generation projects, the Act exempted these proposed projects from the Planning Act. This exemption meant that local governments lost their power to control, amend, or reject projects . This initiative was ultimately reversed after significant backlash . In 2013, under the Kathleen Wynne Liberal government, the Investment Ready Program was introduced. The program aimed to show prospective developers sites in municipalities ready to be developed, outlining information surrounding environmental concerns, utilities, and servicing. This program was described as a mechanism to promote communities, as well as to attract new investments to foster economic and population growth (Peterborough This Week, 2013). In August of that same year, the government announced funding plans of up to 90,000 for each local government to build energy plans. The proposal would allow a local government the opportunity to lay out its preferences for types of energy infrastructure, money saving techniques, promotion of conservation, and other types of local energy planning. The document in question was criticized for not letting local governments veto energy projects, specifically wind farms . The Wynne government proposed doubling the municipal portion of the provincial gas tax in July 2017, with the funds intended for transit . The election of Doug Ford's Conservative government in 2018 returned to a period of provincial downloading to local governments, provincial budget austerity measures, and potential local government restructuring. In 2019, the provincial government was criticized for downloading by stealth by various municipal actors (Morden, 2020; The Peterborough Examiner, 2019). Having planned around the expectation of financial support increasing due to a prior announcement under the Wynne government, local governments were put under stress as the 2019 provincial budget called for local government cuts well after they had passed their own annual budget . For example, the provincial government decreased their contribution to the cost sharing of municipal health boards by approximately 20 . This downloading was expected to save the provincial government 200 million a year. The budget also introduced decreases from regional tourism agencies (reduction of 17.5 million per year), land ambulance and emergency services (reduction of 7.7 million per year), Ontario Municipal Partnership Fund (reduction of 5 million per year), conservation authorities (reduction of 3.7 million), and Ontario Community Infrastructure Fund (reduction of 100 million per year). Further, the Ford government returned the fiscal responsibility for a number of programs (e.g., childcare, public health, and ambulance services) back to local governments (Flare , 2019). The Ford government further commenced a review of the functions of local governments to examine where efficiencies might be made to increase the effectiveness of taxpayer dollars. This review created confusion and panic among local governments with institutional memory, awaiting a potential re visit of local amalgamation and the expected disarray that accompanied it . The review concluded that the best approach was to partner with local governments and to support local decision making, abandoning ideas of amalgamations . Local government restructuring and amalgamation not only served to under represent many rural areas of Ontario, it was ineffective in its intended purpose. Rural local governments were disproportionately impacted by government restructuring and the reduction of spending, if not obsolete, was marginal at best (Douglas, 2005; Kushner and Siegel, 2003; Spicer, 2001). The ebbs and flows of provincial policies have cast Ontario into a position where local governments respond to this lived memory, either through attempts to recoup the damage done through uploading responsibilities back to the provincial level, providing additional revenue streams for municipalities or stealth downloading through a variety of tactics, including but not limited to incrementalism (Morden, 2020; The Peterborough Examiner, 2019; Douglas, 2005). This background ultimately reinforces the original idea of local government being at the mercy of Queen's Park. The New Public Management themes of marketization and managerialism are found throughout the Ontario policy landscape for local governments. Marketization themes of contracting out of services and striving for cost efficiencies noted by Gruening and Torfing . 180 GIBSON AND DALE15410064, 2023, 1, Downloaded from by Toronto Metropolitan Universit, Wiley Online Library on . See the Terms and Conditions ( on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License are clearly seen in policy and funding announcements impacting local governments. The policy changes of Megaweek illustrate both of these themes. The belt tightening of financial resources, the proposed cost savings of amalgamation, and more recent changes to funding formulas for health services, further exemplify the cost efficiency theme. The past 30 years cannot be characterized solely as a period of downloading. Although this is a dominant theme, there are examples of policies and responsibilities uploaded or re uploaded to the provincial government . Managerialism themes of New Public Management identified by Bevir , Funck and Karlson , and Torfing . are also observable in the changing Ontario policy landscape. Initiatives have focused on removing bureaucratic inefficiencies, strategic management, and the encouragement of entrepreneurial management. A Guide to Municipal Restructuring (Ontario Ministry of Municipal Affairs and Housing, 1996) strived to trim bureaucratic fat to make best use of public funds. The influence of New Public Management can be seen throughout the past 30 years of policies influencing rural local governments. The ebbs and flows of provincial policy have created a difficult landscape for rural Ontario local governments, which in many instances have been disproportionately impacted. The continued changes in downloading of responsibilities create uncertainty for long term planning. The multiple changes in provincial policies and responsibilities has led to a do more, with less approach, whereby local governments have increased responsibilities with limited or decreased human and financial resources. METHO DO LOGY Using an exploratory design, this research reviewed academic and policy publications and conducted key informant interviews to examine the impacts of the changing policies on rural local governments in Ontario. As part of a cross country, multi year research initiative, a detailed national and provincial literature review and content analysis of academic literature on rural local government and policy changes impacting rural communities was conducted. This literature review identified key themes which guided local government selection in key informant interviews. An in depth Ontario literature was also conducted to create a chronological account of local government responsibilities to provide both narrative focus for these ebbs and flows, while relating historic precedence set to newer developments that might be recounted or elaborated on by informant interviews. Through the literature reviews, local governments in Ontario outwardly exhibiting potential elements of innovative approaches to local government processes and or service delivery were identified. These innovative approaches emerged in response to one or more of the local government reforms previously discussed. Potential innovative approaches were identified through the literature review and grey literature, including local government trade publications and government reports. These innovative approaches assist in understanding the impacts of these policy changes on rural local governments in Ontario. Representative of eight local governments were selected to participate in key informant interviews to examine the realities of rural local government (see Table 1). The sample includes diversity in geography across the province and the structure of local government (county, single tier, upper tier, and lower tier governments). Each of the local governments is a non metropolitan area or predominantly provides services to non metropolitan areas. A total of 15 key informant interviews were conducted with elected local government officials and senior administrative staff from May to July 2021. Individuals were selected based on their knowledge and experience with the local government. Interviews explored recent demographic, economic, and social changes; the organization of local governments; changing responsibilities and their impacts on the local government over the past 30 years; and new partnerships or collaborations to deliver local government programs or responsibilities. Five key themes emerged from the interviews, each contributing to the understanding of rural local government realities. REALITIES OF RURAL LOCAL GOVERNMENTS Discussions with rural local governments identified a series of five common challenges and opportunities related to the shifting policy landscape: (i) infrastructure pressures, housing, economic development, regional collaboration and partnerships, and (v) fiscal levers. Each of these themes are presented below. Infrastructure pressures Interviewees identified multiple challenges to addressing the demand for new infrastructure and existing infrastructure pressures. Complicating these challenges are a series of policies noted as hindering their abilities to meet the infrastructure demands and pressures. Interviewees from all communities, regardless of growing or declining populations, noted struggles in keeping infrastructural assets updated and described their infrastructure as being stressed. All interviewees noted long term infrastructural deficits and struggles to replace dated infrastructure. Recently required asset management plans were viewed as a useful tool to assess current infrastructural assets, but do not assist in generating the necessary funding to overcome the identified deficits. Local governments struggle with managing infrastructure assets in large geographical areas with small tax bases, their representatives stressing a need for funding from higher levels of government. These infrastructure pressures manifested in multiple ways. Participant 2 noted, bridges had to be closed for a number of years before the Township could afford to replace them that was an example as a result of the Harris era. Further, Participant 7 described the human capacity challenges, We're expanding our infrastructure and still trying to provide services with the same amount of staff. We're looking after much more, much more infrastructure than before, that becomes a pressure. Interviewees from communities experiencing population growth described challenges keeping up with infrastructure demands, particularly around wastewater, housing, and land availability for development. Interviewees explained their ability to address these infrastructure pressures was hindered by existing provincial policies, such as the Provincial Policy Statement and the Municipal Act. In one community with a provincial mandate for population growth the interviewee explained that larger capacity for wastewater treatment is necessary and assistance from the province is a struggle. Participant 10 noted, we have no place to actually plug the new growth. The representative from a second community noted a high demand for new housing to accommodate growing workforce demands and a lack of land within the community's boundaries for new housing developments. The ability to transfer provincial Crown lands adjacent to the community would alleviate pressures. This endeavour, if agreed to, is estimated to take multiple years of planning. Frustration emerged when locally identified strategies for addressing infrastructure pressures run afoul of provincial and federal policies or take significant time for decisions to be made, such as the Provincial Policy Statement or transfers of Crown land. Interviewees noted inheriting new responsibilities for infrastructure management, which created financial and human resources challenges. Recent federal guidelines on chlorine residue in residential wastewater effluent management created new requirements for local governments. The quick turnaround time for compliance required many local governments to take immediate action in upgrading wastewater treatment plants and processes. Participant 13 referred to this as an unfunded mandate another government making decisions that impact municipalities with no consideration of how municipalities are going to respond to or fund. Despite these trends, some local governments are managing to leverage their relationships with neighbouring municipalities and First Nations to expand important infrastructure like water, share infrastructural knowledge, or to introduce new services. Although broadband is not a mandated responsibility of local government, many interviewees noted taking leadership roles in the creation and implementation of broadband initiatives. For example, in Dubreuilville, the Community Networks initiative is creating broadband internet service delivery in a region not currently serviced by existing telecommunications companies. The initiative is a collaboration of four municipalities and five First Nations and was described as a lesson in regional collaboration, inter government collaboration, as well as economic reconciliation (Participant 5). Housing Housing challenges confronted all local governments in the research. Many participants identified struggles with developing housing stock, specifically affordable housing, to meet the demands of current and prospective residents. Further, interviewees noted challenges associated with labour and infrastructure required to support residential development, such as clearing trees, and installing water, wastewater, and roads. 182 GIBSON AND DALE15410064, 2023, 1, Downloaded from by Toronto Metropolitan Universit, Wiley Online Library on . See the Terms and Conditions ( on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License Interviewees stressed their limited tax base did not allow for appropriate revenue generating opportunities to fully cover new residential development expenses. The housing situation has negatively impacted local businesses in their ability to recruit new employees, pushed existing residents out of the local market, and discouraged young families from living in the community. Local government participants described tensions between housing and the protection of agricultural lands. Interviewees explained the Provincial Policy Statement limits their ability to re zone and subdivide agricultural land for new housing developments. Other interviewees noted they have no land left within their municipal boundary for new residential development. Future developments would involve expanding municipal boundaries through annexation or transfer of provincial Crown lands. At the same time, interviewees identified a number of strategies to address housing challenges. Local governments have revised their official plan to allow for secondary suites to generate more housing options. Another local government is in the process of exploring a community land trust to facilitate appropriate housing development for the community. The land trust would protect land for future development, allowing the local government the ability to determine the type of housing development in the area. Economic development In the early 2000s, provincial legislation was introduced to allow local governments to be meaningfully engaged in economic development (Chadwick Parkes, 2008; Siegel, 2011). The 2 Municipal Act allowed local governments to create business counselling services, leasing of land and infrastructure to small business (less than 100 employees), and the establishment of community development corporations . The implication of this policy change was described by Participant 12, 10 years ago, we didn't invest in economic development, because it wasn't considered a core municipal function. Now, it definitely is one of the ones that is most active. The experiences in economic development among participating communities ranged from hiring of economic development staff, creating economic development strategies, implementing Community Improvement Plans, and working with employers on workforce development strategies. The economies of rural Ontario have historically been centered on natural resources based industries. In recent decades, rural economies have shifted. Participants from local governments noted the composition of their community's economy was evolving, such as Sioux Lookout witnessing gradual shifts towards service and creative economies and Huron County seeing the emergent focus on value added industries, including breweries and wineries. Local government participants identified several economic development challenges. Interviewees noted they would like to be more engaged in innovative strategies with the private and voluntary sectors to help resolve local challenges and build new opportunities. Interviewees expressed frustration at the Municipal Act's limitation on these types of initiatives, particularly noting the concern of bonusing or the provision of assistance to private sector actors through activities such as lending property, loan guarantees, and exemptions from charges. This policy was seen as discouraging innovative strategies. Local governments are engaged in a range of economic development initiatives and feasibility studies. One local government is considering the creation of an economic development commission. The commission would receive some core funding from the local government and would need to seek additional funds to implement activities. Another local government is working with regional partners to explore a hydrogen energy initiative. This green energy initiative would convert excess energy to hydrogen for export and create local jobs. Local government restructuring, local capacity, and regional collaboration The experiences of local governments with amalgamation and restructuring have varied with equally mixed reviews to accompany them. Participant 13 noted, municipalities are still struggling with and adjusting to some of that, some of those realities, because it made for some significant changes. The long term impacts of local government restructuring, and influences of New Public Management, were evident in all rural local governments. Although the CSR and associated downloading attempted to cut down on the costs of bureaucracy, many amalgamated municipalities faced the upkeep and maintenance of duplicate, non centralized infrastructures and services. For example, the Township of Brock now oversees three separate libraries, town halls, and ice surfaces under the local government's jurisdiction. Communities are either forced to budget to support everything or have to make difficult decisions surrounding the flow and centralization of funding as infrastructure ages and becomes a cost burden to an already small taxpayer base. Other local governments de amalgamated, such as Haldimand County and its now neighbour, Norfolk, after an order from the government to make municipalities smaller, essentially transforming into a single tier government overnight with a full slate of responsibilities attached. Rural local governments are experiencing increasing responsibilities that outpace the size of available human resources, with bare bones used to describe local human capacity (Participants 1, 4). Participant 5 noted, the province continually downloads regulatory issues we have to handle. But over and above that, we are expected to come up with innovative solutions that serve the private sector players in our neighborhood. We're really a small team, so we do the best we can with what we have. Interviewees described concerns about the level of DO MORE, WITH LESS: THE REALITIES OF LOCAL GOVERNMENT IN RURAL ONTARIO 18315410064, 2023, 1, Downloaded from by Toronto Metropolitan Universit, Wiley Online Library on . See the Terms and Conditions ( on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License capacity within the local government to continue the current requirements, let alone handle any further downloading of responsibilities or explore innovative opportunities. Given limited human resources, interviewees described regional collaborations as important for service provision and efficient use of limited financial and human resources. Collaborations took many forms, ranging from regional service provisions (e.g., garbage, water), bulk purchasing initiatives, and knowledge sharing among government staff. Interviewees noted the value of these regional collaborations were threefold: lower expense for each local government, better quality service, and compliance with all necessary policy and regulations. Large distances between communities complicated regional collaborations for communities in northern Ontario. Although involving larger distances, local governments also highlighted collaborations with actors outside their regions which serve to enhance their communities. The interviewee from Dubreuilville noted a partnership with researchers at Laurentian University in Sudbury to assist with the local government's recent strategic planning processes. A representative from Sioux Lookout described a recent initiative focused on enhancing innovation with researchers at Lakehead University and the University of Toronto. Human resources, however, also limit the amount of collaboration local governments can meaningfully engage. Fiscal levers The fiscal levers provided to local governments were described as dated, limited, and a barrier to creating innovative local strategies. Local governments have limited mechanisms for new revenue generation. Interviewees noted small industrial and residential tax bases cannot continue to carry high tax levels. This creates difficult situations for local governments: it's a never ending struggle to try to find that balance where we're able to provide programs and services to the levels that the public demands but also trying to do it in a way that you know kind of we're able to hold the line as much as possible, on tax increases (Participant 13). To complicate the situation, Participant 3 noted, we're totally beholden to those provincial transfers our fortunes rise and fall with the support of the provincial government. Local government participants noted that they are exploring revenue diversification options, with many undertaking feasibility studies. Examples of non tax revenue diversifications included ownership of power utilities, renting out facilities, purchasing of property and charging rent, and purchasing and operating of previous federal or provincial assets such as airports and ports. The current fiscal reality generates an environment of a low risk tolerance. Interviewees noted the Municipal Act discourages creative strategies for revenue diversification. DISCUSSION Ontario's 30 years of ebbs and flows in local government policy has impacted the authority, responsibilities, and financial capacities of rural local governments. This policy landscape is characterized by increasing responsibilities (both financial and human resources), stagnant or decreased financial resources to implement responsibilities, and the need for new approaches. As noted by Graham and Phillips (1998, ), Ontario has been the site of some of the most turbulent provincial local relations ever experienced in a Canadian province. Eidelman . estimate local governments now need to navigate over 280 provincial policies, regulations, and policy frameworks. The ebbs and flows experienced by rural local governments create an overall environment of uncertainty for long term planning. The key themes of New Public Management are evident throughout the local government interviews (see Table 2). The themes of performance based decision making and public private partnerships were both noted in the discussions around economic development and the processes of restructuring, capacity, and collaboration. The managerialism themes of decentralization and entrepreneurial management were evident in all five research themes as well. The theme of citizens as clients was specifically mentioned in the restructuring, capacity, and collaboration section. The intended outcomes of Ontario's local government policies are focused on the adoption of businesses practices in the public sector, financial efficiencies, re organizing of responsibilities to lower levels of government, restructuring, and a focus on outputs over process. Key themes of New Public Management identified in the literature review emerged in the interview analysis. This research highlights the multiple impacts of continual policy changes on rural local governments in Ontario. The decisions of successive provincial government have led to the do more, with less approach currently faced by local governments in rural Ontario. Operating in a landscape of over 200 policies and regulations, elected officials and senior staff of rural local governments shared their realities, concerns, and strategies for meeting the regulatory requirements. The actions of rural local governments highlight a strong sense of commitment to the future of their communities, frustrations with increasing responsibilities, innovative approaches, and suggestions for policy change. As Participant 13 proclaimed, municipalities need to be recognized as capable what we need is more legislative flexibility to be able to make those decisions to be able to be more creative and entrepreneurial and innovative. As Tindal . note, local governments continue to be the site of reactive solutions rather than sites of proactive, placed based solutions designed by local actors to meet local priorities. Place based approaches require innovative and entrepreneurial rural local governments . This Ontario policy landscape of downloading, limited human and financial resources, and changing authority has created, perhaps necessitated, opportunities for local governments to seek alternative strategies to deliver programs and services. As Participant 5 noted, there's not going to be anybody riding in on a shining horse, or a white horse, with a bucket full of money for us. Solutions to the challenges encountered by rural local governments need to be locally derived in partnership with senior levels of governments. This research advances our understanding of the realities of rural local governments, including the challenges, opportunities, and suggestions for policy revision. Additional research is required to examine how rural local governments are utilizing innovative and entrepreneurial approaches within the current policy landscape to mitigate risks and enhance their community's prosperity. to get cities out of their constitutional straitjacket.pdf","displayName":"How to get cities out of their constitutional straitjacket.pdf","objectPath":"/local/uploads/1775479379755-How_to_get_cities_out_of_their_constitutional_straitjacket.pdf","contentType":"application/pdf","size":1149679,"folder":"week-6-cppa122-reading","listened":false,"lastChunkIndex":0,"totalChunks":8,"checkedChunks":null,"ttsAudioUrl":null,"ttsGeneratedAt":null,"extractedText":"How to get cities out of their constitutional straitjacket Constitutional change could be done province-by-prov- ince, but even short of that, there are tools to keep prov- inces from overpowering municipalities. JUNE 15, 2 BY ALEXANDRA FLYNN NATHALIE DES ROSIERS RICHARD ALBERT Sunrise in Prince Albert, Saskatchewan. Shutterstock.com We need our cities to succeed. They are drivers of the economy. They are the first point of contact for social services. Cities are on the frontlines against hunger, homelessness, inequality and other pressing problems. But cities today do not have all the tools they need to help improve their neighbourhoods and communities. Cities and their residents have been calling for reform more money, more innovation, better leadership for decades. The biggest problem standing in the way of cities is the former British North America Act, a foundation of our constitutional system, written at a time when urban areas represented only 20 per cent of the population, far from the 80 per cent of today. Times have changed, but even after the major constitutional reforms introduced in 1982, Canada still treats cities as though we are in 1867. Five simple words in the Constitution Act, 1982 have put cities in a straitjacket. Under section 92, provinces have exclusive jurisdiction over Municipal institutions in the Province. In short, what a province gives to cities, it may take away, without much explanation why. This leaves cities with little capacity to plan, limited power to build the fiscal capacity to deliver improved social services and fully at the mercy of provincial politicians who often have little if any experience in municipal matters. What makes this even worse is the democratic deficit: electoral district rules commonly squeeze many more people into urban ridings than in rural ridings, diluting the vote of Canadians living in cities. There are many reasons for the crisis of governance that impedes the work of cities, but the proximate cause is the subservient status of cities in the Constitution. The Canadian model of municipal government There are many things that could be done today to address these issues. Provinces could agree to grant more power and taxation authority to their cities. There could also be court rulings on the limits of provincial power over cities. But in the end, it might be necessary to have constitutional change, even if it s incremental and on a province-by-province basis. The Canadian model of municipal government is not widely shared. In many other countries, cities have constitutional authority to do what their residents need them to do. These cities solve social problems, they work collaboratively as partners with other orders of government, they have far more fiscal powers in their toolkits, and they are thriving centres of democratic, artistic, economic and social innovation. In Canada, our cities are seen as service providers, not governments. As a result, Canadian cities must beg from, and bend to, provinces to do virtually everything, and certainly anything new. Municipal empowerment is not an intractable problem. Throughout the world, and in the Global South particularly, good local governance is embraced as a political and democratic necessity. In Mexico, South Africa and within the European Union, constitutional frameworks are understood as dynamic, not rigid. Canada is lagging far behind in appreciating all the good things that cities can bring to the country as equal partners in modern governance. The bottom line is this: the legal status of cities as creatures of the provinces is untenable. Were we writing our Constitution today, we would not recreate the same structure for cities, with their existence depending on the goodwill of provincial governments. There is no good reason why this should endure any longer. Kenora, Ont. at sunset. Shutterstock.com Empowering cities without amending the Constitution In April 2021, we hosted the Massey Cities Summit, bringing together dozens of community leaders, elected representatives and scholars in a three-day conference to brainstorm how to give cities more power without amending the Constitution. Here are a few takeaways. First, no constitution is static. The Canadian Constitution is, as judges have called it, a living tree. Its interpretation is meant to evolve over time, making way for new ideas to improve governance and democratic outcomes. For example, subsidiarity is a promising organizing theory because it counsels that the level of governance closest to the people should be the one most empowered to act. Subsidiarity can help guide the resolution of conflicts between provincial and municipal actions. But subsidiarity is just one of many theories that can help us out of our constitutional straitjacket. In March 2021, the Supreme Court heard a constitutional challenge to the province of Ontario s decision to dramatically reduce the size of Toronto city council against the city s wishes in the middle of the 2018 municipal election campaign. Toronto, and a dozen intervenors, argued that many municipalities existed before Confederation, that cities are democratic governments, not just creatures of the province, and that Ontario should not limit voting rights during an election. The Supreme Court has not ruled on this yet, but these are promising arguments that courts can use to help our Constitution evolve as our needs for improved local governance grow. Second, there are political tools at our disposal. Stricter legislative language could limit provinces from overpowering municipal councils. For example, requirements for special parliamentary majorities could signal that provincial power must be exercised in a way that supports, rather than undercuts, local self-government. Enlightened provinces should see that the future depends on strong municipalities that can address crises in climate change, poverty or affordable housing provided that cities are given the power to act. Local governments need appropriate and reliable revenues to deliver the municipal services their residents want and need. Here, intergovernmental arrangements can be strengthened to protect municipal autonomy and stabilize funding. Promising options include granting tax points i.e., reducing provincial taxes by a fixed percentage and giving the municipalities the right to raise taxes by similar amount or by giving a fixed percentage of sales taxes to municipalities. Alternatively, or in addition, why not enact municipal equalization payments, just like the provinces get from Ottawa? Municipal equalization would ensure that a fair and reasonable share of sales and income taxes goes to local government. Third, with additional municipal authority must come commensurate responsibilities. The bar must be higher for what counts as good government for empowered cities. Cities must have respectful relationships with First Nations and Indigenous communities located in and around city boundaries. They must recognize the needs of rural areas that feed and nurture cities. They must act deliberatively and democratically. Local autonomy will need to be exercised in the context of the interdependency that characterizes modern life. Greater powers always require greater accountability. The result will be better- trained and better-educated city halls, higher expectations for civic innovation and real, meaningful engagement with residents. These takeaways are exciting, but they will go nowhere unless provinces are willing to go the distance to recognize the importance of cities. Constitutional change, one province at a time That is why another option must always remain on the table: constitutional change. The problem with a constitutional amendment to give more powers to all cities in Canada is that our Constitution is exceedingly hard to modify in that kind of overall context perhaps the most difficult in the world to change. That kind of change requires approval from both the Senate and the House of Commons, seven out of 10 provinces with at least 50 per cent of the Canadian population, and, quite likely, a national referendum as well. On top of all that, politicians are reluctant to reopen the Constitution after the failures of the Meech Lake and Charlottetown accords. Fortunately, we might not need a Canada-wide constitutional amendment to We could proceed one province at a time, authorizing city charters in each, using the Constitution s amending procedure in section 43. This section authorizes amendments affecting only one province to be approved by that province and both houses of Parliament a much more manageable threshold. A province may also amend its own constitution under section 45 by a vote of its legislature, without federal or other approvals although the contour of this power is still unknown. We are not lacking in options. In our view, the urgency of the problem means that all options should be considered both those that keep us within the current constitutional framework and those requiring alterations. The need for change has never been more dire. Cities are expected to respond to the growing needs of their residents in the wake of the pandemic, the climate emergency and massive social inequities. It is time to give cities the freedom to do the work they can do best. Empowering Canadian cities is a crucial democratic project for us all. Reluctance of provincial governments to share power with municipalities is not surprising, but it must be overcome. Strong municipalities do not make weak provinces. Instead, they lift up entire regions and the country as a whole. A 21 century Canadian federalism needs municipalities at the table now. Alan Kasperski, the conference connector for the 2 Massey Cities Summit, executive producer of the City In Sight podcast, and participatory democracy advocate, also contributed to this article. (Adrian Wyld Canadian Press) comments This column is an opinion by Tomas Hachard, manager of programs and research at the Institute on Municipal Finance and Governance at the University of Toronto's Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy. For more information about CBC's Opinion section, please see the FAQ. Throughout the COVID-19 crisis, Canadian city governments have been on the front lines delivering essential services while struggling with limited fiscal resources. The pressures of the pandemic have made it clear that there are cracks in Canada's federal structure, particularly in relation to cities. Menu Search Sign In Even though city governments are growing in importance and responsibility, they remain \"little siblings\" in Canadian federalism, often ignored by Ottawa or overruled by the provinces. This imbalance has repercussions for all Canadians. Canada is one of the most decentralized countries on the planet, and little can be accomplished without ensuring all governments are equipped to make the decisions and sustain the investments Canada requires for its future success. As I note in research for the Institute on Municipal Finance and Governance, cities face four particular challenges because of the imbalance in intergovernmental relations. The first is paternalism. Cities have a semblance of authority in several policy areas, but often little actual power to make changes. For example, depending on where you live in Canada, changes to speed limits may require provincial approval, local public health decision-making is second-guessed, and municipal planning decisions can be appealed to provincially regulated oversight bodies, as can policing budget decisions. Saskatoon ICUs maxed out because of COVID-19, patients diverted to smaller centres What's open and closed in Halifax as COVID-19 restrictions ramp up The second challenge is constrained finances. Cities have inadequate sources of revenue and insufficient fiscal flexibility to meet their responsibilities. One consequence of this is city plans or actions that, without provincial and federal funding, simply can't proceed. The biggest effect is on infrastructure, and particularly transit, where many cities can't afford their repair bills, let alone the cost of new construction or needed expansion. The third challenge is poor coordination. Unclear and overlapping jurisdiction between orders of government leads to inefficient programs and disputes over responsibility. In Ontario, this challenge has recently been epitomized by debates over what power cities have to enact public health restrictions on their own. The final challenge is fragmentation. Many of the most visionary ideas for the future of cities are best implemented at a metropolitan scale. Housing and transit challenges, for example, cross municipal borders and affect entire metropolitan regions. Yet in most of Canada, metropolitan regions are made up of several municipalities, and inadequate governance structures exist to allow for effective coordination. How can these challenges be addressed? First, a clarification of the powers and responsibilities of modern cities is needed. Canada currently suffers from conflicted and contradictory answers to the questions of what municipal governments ought to be and what they ought to do. If city governments are increasingly significant public policymakers, they need to have the resources, autonomy, and institutions appropriate to deliver on that role. A principles-based review of provincial-municipal relations to clarify who does what and how we pay for it would help ensure that city governments are able to meet the expectations we have for them. Health experts in B.C. divided over merits of severe Australian-style lockdown COVID-19 lockdowns brought in for Toronto and Peel, but not York Of course, Canadian provinces and territories are also strained by the current balance of intergovernmental relations. Any review of provincial-municipal responsibilities would need to take into account the federal-provincial territorial context. The pandemic has required closer co-operation between federal officials such as Health Minister Patty Hajdu, right, premiers such as Ontario's Doug Ford, left, and municipal officials. (Chris Young, Adrian Wyld Canadian Press) Second, relations between the federal, provincial territorial and municipal governments in Canada need to be deepened. Many of Canada's greatest policy challenges require increased coordination and cooperation among all three orders of government. However, there exists no mechanism for ongoing, formal federal-provincial-municipal relations. Cities, provinces, and the federal government need formal avenues for collaborative governance. Established committees that include mayors and city managers, and their counterparts at the provincial and federal levels, would create avenues for ongoing cooperation. It is not feasible for every Canadian municipality to be at the intergovernmental table, but that gap could be filled by metropolitan institutions that represent city-regions, or by municipal associations in each province. At the same time, governments should pursue trilateral agreements to address policy challenges that require coordinated action and multi-level funding. Such agreements could be modelled on the urban development agreements in Vancouver and Winnipeg, which brought together government and community partners, and led to funding for economic development and neighbourhood revitalization. Fundamentally, in a policy area like mental health which involves every order of government, because it intersects with housing, the opioid crisis, health care, and policing trilateral agreements could coordinate existing work being done by individual governments, and direct resources to where they are most needed. As COVID-19 surges, Alberta braces for possible new restrictions More provinces sign up for rent benefit as Ottawa sets up promised housing council There have been debates about how much power municipal, provincial and federal levels of government have when deciding on measures to prevent the spread of COVID-19 and enforcing them. (Adrian Wyld The Canadian Press) Making all this happen is no easy feat, and it requires give-and-take from every level of government, but it's essential if we truly want to fix the obvious cracks in Canadian federalism. In combination, these measures would not only put cities on a firmer footing, they would also ensure more effective funding, coordination, and delivery of public services across all orders of government. Canada will be better able to \"build back better\" from COVID-19, address climate change, reform social policy, and improve health care if the governments best able to deliver on specific aspects of these efforts can afford to take them on. With better coordination and cooperation between all three orders of government, Canada will be better equipped to handle the challenges ahead. This column is part of CBC's Opinion section. In today's Western society with increasing sexual stimuli on one hand and growing awareness of the risks of sexual victimization on the other, parents and educators find it difficult to decide how to react to sexual behaviors and questions about sexuality from children One of the very basic concepts of this course is that human beings are sexual beings from birth until death. This life-span approach acknowledges that throughout our entire lives we are in a constant state of evolution and development. As a key component of who we are, our sexuality also develops and evolves from infancy until the end of our lives. Increasingly, researchers believe that the development of sexuality in childhood plays an important role shaping our sexuality as adolescents and adults. For example, if as children growing up, we continually receive the message that our bodies (particularly the genitals) and sexual feelings are shameful, it seems logical that we might be more likely to have difficulty forming healthy and satisfying sexual relationships later in life. Consequently, we will begin our examination of sexuality over the life course by looking at childhood. This topic overview will outline some of the key points you will need to be aware of in examining the topic of childhood sexuality and introduce you to the two required readings for this module. Key Point The development of sexuality in childhood forms the building blocks for the development of sexuality in adolescence and adulthood. One of the first things you will discover in researching this topic is that we know far less about sexuality in childhood than we do about sexuality in any other phase of life. Key Point Compared other phases of life (i.e., adolescence, adulthood) we know very little about the development of sexuality in childhood. Why do we know relatively little about the development of sexuality in childhood? One reason is that there are some methodological obstacles to research on childhood sexuality. For example, much of the research that has been conducted on adolescents and adults with respect to sexuality is derived from self-report questionnaires where subjects are asked to report their sexual opinions, feelings, motivations, and behaviours. This is nearly impossible to do with children, particularly young children. For one thing, as you will learn from your readings in this module, children typically do not interpret their feelings and behaviours as being sexual in nature in the way that a teenager or adult would. For example a child who gets physical pleasure from touching his or her genitals will not think of this as a sexual activity (i.e., masturbation). They simply think of it as something that feels good. In addition, a child's level of cognitive development makes it difficult to develop, implement, and interpret results from self-report questionnaires. An additional problem is that given general societal attitudes towards childhood sexuality (more on this later), researchers often have difficulty getting permission to ask children about their sexual feelings and behaviours. Another possibility is to observe children in natural settings such as daycare's, playgrounds, and schools. Although observational research can and does provide useful information on the sexuality related behaviour of children it is limited by the fact that children learn quite early in life that such behaviour is best done in private, away from the prying eyes of adults including parents and educators. Yet another possibility is to ask teenagers or adults to recall their sexuality related feelings and behaviours during childhood. However, asking people to accurately recall feelings and behaviours that occurred many years in the past is never a very precise way of measuring things. This is particularly so with sexuality since as a seven year-old you may have interpreted a particular feeling or behaviour quite differently than you would now. Nevertheless, despite these limitations, the available research does provide us with a reasonable, if somewhat speculative, picture of sexual development in the childhood years. Before we proceed to these findings it is important to first take a look at societal attitudes towards childhood sexuality. By the end of this module students will be able to: 1. Describe and evaluate societal attitudes towards childhood sexuality and sexual behaviour. 2. Identify the key developmental tasks related to sexuality for children aged 0-2, 2-5, 5-8, and 9-12. 3. Describe common sexual behaviours among children at different ages. 4. Distinguish between child sexual behaviours that are considered healthy and those that are cause for concern. Societal Attitudes Toward Childhood Sexuality In North American culture, the sexuality of children is a topic that many adults are generally uncomfortable acknowledging or talking about, especially when it comes to talking to children themselves. We have all heard stories about parents being nervous about having the \"birds and the bees\" talk with their children. For a number of reasons, the concept of childhood \"sexual innocence\" or asexuality permeates our culture . The quote from Oprah in the box below exemplifies the false belief that children have no inherent sexuality until they are exposed to it in some way in the environment. \"Once you are exposed to sex - you're never able to regain innocence again - from then on you have sexual thoughts - you have sexual feelings - innocence is forever gone. It encourages sexual curiosity that would not have been there\" Oprah Winfrey. The Oprah Winfrey Show, January 6, 1988. Although many, if not most, parents who observe their toddlers touching themselves and other children in seemingly sexual ways consider such behaviours as harmless, some parents will actively discourage their children's curiosity about sexuality. Others will choose to simply ignore their child's sexual development by not taking opportunities to talk to their children about their bodies and their sexuality. Sexologist Ira Reiss suggests that, For parents not to face the reality of child sexual exploration is to forgo a major opportunity for a positive input into shaping their child's future sexuality. The very acts of denying child sexuality, trying to limit it, and not discussing sex give the child the clear message that sexuality has something taboo and negative associated with it. Childhood is the perfect time for parents to give their children permission to explore sexuality, to give them a positive view about it, to open up a dialogue, and to help prepare them for establishing their future sexual relationships (). Clearly, increasing numbers of parents are adopting a more positive approach to child sexuality. Still, it is also clear that many parents are reluctant to talk to their young children about sexuality related matters or are uncertain about how much sexuality information they should be giving to their children. A study of parents in New Brunswick revealed that 60 had not discussed the concept of sexual pleasure with their children in grades 6 to 8. For parents with children in grades 4-5, 78 had not discussed this topic. In addition, 55 of parents with children in grades K to 3 had discussed the correct names for genitals \"not at all\" or in \"general terms only\" (Weaver, Byers, Sears, Cohen, and Randall, 2002). Interestingly, although many parents are reluctant to talk to their own kids about sex, a number of Canadian studies have found that most parents are in favour of providing elementary age children with some form of sexuality education in the schools (e.g., McKay ., 2014; SIECCAN, 2020; Wood , 2021). For example, Wood . found that most parents approved of schools teaching children about the correct names for their genitals in Grade 5 or earlier and over half approved teaching about a range of topics in Grades 6 to 8 or earlier including: gender identity, gender roles and stereotypes, sexual orientation, media literacy skills related to sexuality content in advertising, TV, pornography etc., information about masturbation, and personal safety (e.g., abuse prevention). Key Point Although many parents are reluctant to talk to their children about sexuality, most parents are in favour of providing sexuality education in the schools at Grades 6 to 8 or earlier. Simply put, North American society appears to have ambivalent or mixed feelings about childhood sexuality. It should be noted at this point that in Scandinavian countries a much more liberal approach to informing children about sexuality prevails. For example, in a study examining childhood sexuality in the 1980s in different industrialized countries it was found that at age nine 60 of Swedish children, compared to only 4 of North American children, were aware that enjoyment is one of the reasons people have intercourse . It would be interesting to see if the results would be different if this study was conducted now. ...it is clear that parents in the United States observe less sexual behavior in their children than parents in the Netherlands or Sweden. It is not clear however whether this means that these children really display less sexual behavior, hide their behavior better, or that these parents are less willing to perceive or report sexual behavior in their children. Another possible explanation is that parents who report less sexual behavior do see their children touching their genitals, but do not perceive this behavior to be sexual (Graaf and Rademakers, 2006, 17). Why is North American society relatively uncomfortable with childhood sexuality? It is likely that much of our discomfort with, or ambivalence toward childhood sexuality is a remnant of the Restrictive sexual ideology that has governed Western culture for most of our history. As we saw in Module 1, Restrictive sexual ideology tends to view sexuality with suspicion. According to Restrictive sexual ideology, unless carefully controlled, sexual feelings and desires have a strong potential to result in negative outcomes. From this perspective, signs of sexual feelings or behaviours among children represent a permanent loss of innocence - or worse - are an indication that the child has become harmfully preoccupied with something that children should, by nature, have no interest in. According to Restrictive sexual ideology children are, in most respects asexual, without sexual feelings or desires. Thus, curiosity about sexuality among children is to be discouraged. In this view there is no need for children to learn about sexuality from either their parents or from the schools. Indeed, such education is seen as harmful, not helpful. While it would clearly be an exaggeration to suggest that most North American adults agree with this approach, there is little doubt that our cultural heritage of Restrictive sexual ideology is still with us to some extent as it applies to childhood sexuality. All cultures have strong incest taboos which may serve to inhibit explicit educational discussions between children and their parents about sexuality. However, the incest taboo does not seem to have prevented adults in other societies from taking a more liberal approach to educating children about sexuality. Key Point Compared to other cultures, North American culture takes a restrictive approach to childhood sexuality. The Importance of Childhood Sexuality Education Why is it important to help children learn about sexuality? What are the potentially negative consequences of attempting to keep children \"in the dark\" with respect to sexuality? As noted above, in important respects, the seeds of adult sexual health are planted in childhood. Children who grow up ignorant about sexuality or associate sexuality with shame may be more likely to experience difficulty with sexuality in adolescence and childhood. For example, children who are taught from an early age about only the negative aspects of human sexuality and are scolded for any expression of sexuality may grow up with what are referred to as erotophobic attitudes and emotions. They begin to feel guilty and fearful about sexuality. An erotophobic individual has not accepted themselves as a sexual being and as a consequence may have difficulty forming healthy sexual relationships or take the necessary steps to protect themselves from HIV STI infection. In addition, children who are ignorant about sexuality may be more vulnerable to sexual exploitation and abuse. For example, a child who has no knowledge about sexuality may be less aware that it is inappropriate for an adult to touch them in a sexual way. In other words, they may be less able to distinguish between \"good touch\" and \"bad touch\". Another issue to consider is that there can be no doubt that our culture is increasingly saturated with sexual imagery, whether its on television, the internet or other source. It would be virtually impossible for even the most vigilant parent to prevent their child from being exposed, in one way or another, to various forms of sexuality related content. It is also apparent that much of this material, particularly on the internet, is inaccurate or sends unhealthy messages about sexuality. Effective childhood sexuality education by parents, caregivers, and teachers can help children learn important, accurate information and provide guidance that can make a significant contribution to healthy child development. Key Point Effective childhood sexuality education can make an important contribution to healthy child development. What does the limited available research tell us about childhood sexual behaviour? From her review of studies in this area, Larsson identified three very basic conclusions that can be drawn. 1. Children are naturally curious about their own bodies and those of others and can take part in sexual investigations of their own body and in games with other children. Children vary in their interest in sexuality. 2. Behaviours which appear to imitate adult sexuality, e.g. attempted intercourse or imitation of sex with another child or dolls soft toys; attempts to insert objects in the child's own anus or vagina or the anus or vagina of another child; oral genital contact and demanding that others take part in specific sexual activities with the child, are very uncommon in observations of normal groups of children but are more common among children who have been the victims of abuse. 3. Problematic sexual interaction between children seems to be characterised by force threats, dominance, violence, aggression and compulsiveness, unlike sex play which is spontaneous, good-humoured and mutual in nature . Key Point Children are naturally curious about their own bodies and the bodies of others including genitalia. Although children vary in their interest in sexuality, many children will engage in various forms of sexuality related play. Sex play is typically consensual and good humoured whereas problematic childhood sexual behaviours are often characterized by coercion and or appear to be attempts to imitate adult sexual behaviours. Data and replication files for the analyses available at MULTILEVEL POLICY FROM THE MUNICIPAL PERSPECTIVE 2 Introduction Public policy scholars with interests in the institutional dynamics of Canadian public policy have typically focused on the role of federal and provincial governments, and the relations between them, in the policy process (Bakvis and Skogstad 2012, Wallner 2014). In recent years, how- ever, a combination of factors relative quiet on the constitutional file, the heightened salience of complex policy domains in Canadian cities, new attention to Indigenous governance and reconciliation has prompted a new interest in the role of other actors in the policy process, such as munic- ipalities, private actors, Indigenous communities, and NGOs. While these actors are hardly new policy players in Canada, sustained academic at- tention to their role in public policy development and implementation has until recently been the preserve of a small number of pathbreaking schol- ars . Nearly all of the work that has emerged from this new interest in the multilevel dynamics of Canadian policymaking has focused on case studies of policy domains in which multiple actors are clearly engaged in the policy process, such as immigrant settlement (Good 2009, H. Smith 2004, Tolley and Young 2011), emergency planning , or homelessness (Doberstein 2016, A. Smith 2016). What is less clear, at this point, is how these policy domains fit within the broader spectrum of activities in which non-constitutional actors such as municipalities are involved. Are these domains typical of other areas of policy? Is intensive involvement of multiple actors confined to a few high-profile domains, or is it distributed more evenly across a range of policy areas? Is it possi- ble to describe multilevel policy involvement more systematically across policy domains? Our goal in this article is to begin to address these questions. Drawing from a new survey of more than 1,000 mayors and councillors from mu- nicipalities across Canada, we provide a big-picture overview of multilevel policy involvement across eighteen policy domains that involve local gov- ernments to some extent. We then distill our data into a novel measure of multilevel policy involvement, allowing for systematic comparison of mul- tilevel policy dynamics across geography, phases of the policy process, and policy domains. These measures provide us with a valuable first look at multilevel policy involvement from the municipal point of view, and they point the way toward a large-scale comparative approach to multilevel gov- ernance in Canada. Background The study of institutions and public policy in Canada has traditionally fo- cused on federal and provincial governments. Many of Canada s leading 17547121, 2019, 2, Downloaded from by Toronto Metropolitan Universit, Wiley Online Library on . See the Terms and Conditions ( on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License JACK LUCAS AND ALISON SMITH 272 policy scholars have devoted themselves to the question of how policymak- ing works within federal and provincial governments, how the two levels of government interact, and how policymaking authority has been distributed between them. Well-established periodization schemes in the development of federal-provincial interaction and policymaking have given way to ap- proaches that are more sensitive to the ways that federal-provincial interac- tion has evolved differently across policy domains. In most of this work, however whether focused on identifying major types or periods of federalism at an aggregated level or on more disaggregated analysis of spe- cific domains federal and provincial governments loom large as the major institutional players in the analysis (Bakvis and Skogstad 2012, Schertzer 2015, Simeon 2002). The tendency to focus on federal and provincial governments has in turn led scholars to examine policy areas that involve these governments, such as immigration, healthcare, and income security. When local actors such as municipalities and non-governmental organizations are mentioned in these studies of Canadian policymaking, if they are mentioned at all, they tend to enter the narrative as advocates or in the implementation phase. The con- stitutional position of Canadian municipalities as so-called creatures of the provinces plays a major role in these narratives; as Robert Young has written, local authorities are a competence of the provincial governments Provincial governments create them, regulate them, prescribe many of the policies they implement, and, not infrequently, eliminate them through amalgamation (Young 2013: 1). This leads to a tendency to view municipal- ities, in Martin Horak s words, as policy takers, not policy makers, on the intergovernmental stage (Horak 2012: 350). Yet, as both Horak and Young go on to argue, this constitutional picture is too simple to capture the realities of Canadian policymaking. Canadian municipalities are the sites of a vast array of complex policy files, some old and some new, which are characterized by input and involvement by actors outside the traditional federal-provincial nexus (Bradford 2005, H. Smith 2004). Of course, not all policy areas involve municipal governments (just as not all policy areas involve federal or provincial governments). But the lack of attention to the local perspective can lead to an incomplete picture of policymaking in Canada. Canadian municipal politicians have the capacity to leverage media profiles, electoral mandates, implementation responsibil- ities, and even infrastructure ownership into a level of involvement in public policy issues that goes well beyond what one would expect from a creature of the province. Within this context, the multilevel governance approach, which looks not just to formal juris- diction but also to the complexities of actual policy involvement of state and non-state actors, is increasingly valuable for understanding public policy processes in Canada. 17547121, 2019, 2, Downloaded from by Toronto Metropolitan Universit, Wiley Online Library on . See the Terms and Conditions ( on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License MULTILEVEL POLICY FROM THE MUNICIPAL PERSPECTIVE 2 Multilevel governance research brings local and non-governmental actors directly into our understanding of Canadian policymaking. In policy areas where there is some degree of local involvement, Bradford explains the im- portance of the multilevel approach to policy and research. He writes, in order to meet the policy challenges, new relations must be forged among the state, civil society, and the economy, and within the different branches and levels of government. These relations will be less hierarchical, more at- tuned to the needs and aspirations of diverse groups, and better able to use different forms of knowledge (Bradford 2005: 12). Putting this perspective into a concise definition, Horak defines multilevel governance as, a mode of policymaking that involves complex interactions among multiple levels of government and social forces (Horak 2012: 339). Working from this defi- nition, multilevel governance in this article refers not only to different levels of government but also to different sectors; these sectors, notably the private sector and the third sector, are generally conceived of as local (see Horak and Young 2012), but can also span scales or jurisdictions themselves. Studies of multilevel governance have tended to focus on specific pol- icy domains, such as climate change adaptation or emergency management . Outside Canada, a number of researchers have begun to develop measures of key features of multilevel governance, such as political authority, across countries and time. Led by Liesbet Hooghe and Gary Marks, these scholars have systematically tracked the evolving authority of substate governments in 42 countries over nearly 60 years. Their findings demonstrate careful attention to the details of each case while also identifying large-scale trends in the direction of increas- ing regional authority (Hooghe, Marks, and Schakel 2010). This attempt to systematically measure and compare core aspects of multilevel governance serves as a major source of inspiration for the approach that we develop here. A second source of inspiration for our approach in this article is Martin Horak s framework for understanding multilevel governance in Canadian cities. In his informative and important concluding chapter to the 2012 ed- ited volume Sites of Governance, Horak develops an exceptionally useful framework for understanding both the actors (federal, provincial, munic- ipal, and social forces ) and the policy phases (policy advocacy, policy development, resource provision, and policy implementation) involved in multilevel governance processes. This framework enables a form of system- atic mapping of multilevel governance that would previously have been lost amidst the complexity of multilevel governance. One of the most striking aspects of multilevel governance in Canada s big cities, Horak concludes, is the tremendous variety of forms it takes (Horak 2012: 341). In this arti- cle, we seek to build upon Horak s analysis to outline this variety of forms across an even larger array of policy domains and actors. We know that a 17547121, 2019, 2, Downloaded from by Toronto Metropolitan Universit, Wiley Online Library on . See the Terms and Conditions ( on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License JACK LUCAS AND ALISON SMITH 274 number of actors are involved in policy areas such as climate change ad- aptation and immigrant settlement, but what about policy areas that are more traditionally considered local? Is the involvement of multiple actors only seen in certain policy areas or in certain phases of the policy process? To answer these questions, we adapt Horak s framework in this article in three main ways. First, we add one new actor to our survey (regional governments) and divide social forces into two new categories: private businesses and non-governmental organizations. This allows us to more precisely estimate the role of municipal governments (as distinguished from regional governments in some provinces) as well as the role of social forces in the policy process in Canadian municipalities. Second, we focus on just three of Horak s four phases of the policy process. We felt that our survey instrument and sampling frame (described below) would be better equipped to capture formal phases of the policy process (development, re- source provision, and implementation), rather than the rather different as- pects of policy agenda-setting and entrepreneurship associated with policy advocacy. Finally, to bring additional comparative data into Horak s analy- sis, we expand our focus beyond six important policy areas in Canada s big cities the focus of the Horak analysis to a larger list of eighteen policy domains and all Canadian municipalities above 5,000 population. A final note on our framework and argument. Martin Horak has suggested that academic definitions of multilevel governance often pre- suppose coordinated action. Yet the degree to which policy action is actu- ally coordinated in multilevel governance varies widely (). While we agree with Horak, we do not address the extent to which actors at different levels and in different sectors are coordinated in their policy efforts in this article. Rather, we seek to explore, systematically and across an array of pol- icy domains, the involvement of governmental and non-governmental actors in policy areas that involve local governments to some extent in the policy process. Data and methods As we have suggested above, our goal in this article is to begin to outline large-scale comparative patterns of multilevel policy involvement in policy areas that involve local actors, from the perspective of Canadian municipal politicians. Our approach is simple: ask municipal councillors and mayors from across Canada about their perceptions of multilevel policy involve- ment and report what they tell us. In this section, we outline the details and motivation of this research design, including the survey frame, our measure of multilevel policy involvement, and the strengths and weaknesses of the approach. 17547121, 2019, 2, Downloaded from by Toronto Metropolitan Universit, Wiley Online Library on . See the Terms and Conditions ( on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License MULTILEVEL POLICY FROM THE MUNICIPAL PERSPECTIVE 2 Sampling frame and respondents Our findings are drawn from a survey of Canadian mayors and councillors. In March and April of 2018, we distributed a survey invitation by email to a population of 4,578 municipal mayors and councillors from across Canada. To compile the invitation list, we collected the publicly available email ad- dresses for all mayors and councillors in municipalities above 5,000 popula- tion, using census subdivisions in Statistics Canada s 2016 census tables to identify our list of municipalities.1 When email addresses were unavailable, we requested them directly from city clerks. In a handful of municipalities, officials did not respond to our request or (very rarely) refused to provide email addresses. Overall, however, our population list includes nearly every current municipal politician (well over 95 percent of the total) in Canadian municipalities above 5,000 population. We collected data from municipali- ties in all provinces and territories; because of a very small number of re- sponses from the North, however (just seven completed surveys), we exclude the Territories from our analysis in this paper. We chose to survey elected municipal politicians rather than other local actors such as senior municipal administrators for three main reasons. The first is practicality: while collecting the emails of 4,578 involved con- siderable effort, most of the email addresses that we needed were publicly accessible, making it possible to compile our list of respondents without con- tacting hundreds of individual municipalities with email address requests. The same would not be true for chief administrative officers or other senior administrators, whose contact information is often much harder to access. Second, we felt that a survey of elected politicians across Canada would allow for comparability; unlike senior administrators whose roles and job titles vary considerably across municipalities, mayors and councillors are elected in broadly similar ways to serve broadly similar policymaking functions across Canada. This allowed us to probe the association between, say, population size and multilevel policy involvement without needing to add controls for the job titles and roles of our respondents. Finally, and perhaps most importantly, municipal politicians are important players in Canadian multilevel governance; the informal, ad hoc, and non-institu- tionalized patterns of intergovernmental interaction that often characterize multilevel governance in Canada mean that local politicians perceptions provide a vital perspective on who is involved in multilevel policy processes (Bramwell 2014; Miller and Smart 2012; Leo and August 2009). In addition to the politician survey, however, we also received responses from 208 se- nior administrators whose email addresses were readily available in British Columbia; we compare these responses to those of our main respondent pool (elected politicians) in the section below. 17547121, 2019, 2, Downloaded from by Toronto Metropolitan Universit, Wiley Online Library on . See the Terms and Conditions ( on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License JACK LUCAS AND ALISON SMITH 2 A total of 1,084 elected politicians consented to participate in the survey, for an overall completion rate of 24 percent. As in many opt-in full-popula- tion elite surveys, we cannot know how representative our respondents are of the population from which they are drawn. We can, however, check for obvious sources of concern by comparing our respondents to the popula- tion on observable characteristics such as gender, province, and municipal size. While we have no reason to expect that some of these factors, such as gender, are related to opinions on multilevel policy involvement, we can gain confidence about the representativeness of our sample on unobservable characteristics of our respondents by comparing our sample to the popula- tion on characteristics that we are able to observe.
